item.title: SCP-5480:
item.content:encoded:
I hate Sarkic lore. This was pretty entertaining to read as a parody of that. I appreciated it for that and enjoyed the piece.

Two side notes, one for the author and one in general.

First — that's not a rough translation. That translation is pretty straightforward and literal.

Second — given that immortals don't actually exist, I think it's pretty unrealistic of people who constantly try to take umbrage with how they speak. There's a constant demand that their speech patterns never change remotely, even when they are acting like a regular person. If you don't adapt to life in the modern world — and more than anything else, that includes your vernacular and slang — then you'll stick out like a sore thumb in what, fifty years?

item.title: SCP-5480:
item.content:encoded:
The interview log is a bit rough, but I think this hits all the right notes. It's a solid attempt at a parody of Sarkic lore. Though I will say, I have only a passing knowledge of Sarkicism on the Wiki — I've read a few of its articles and know some names, and that's it. So maybe, if I knew less about the subject matter (to the point of not picking up on anything), or more (to the point of being considered a fan of Sarkicism, which I admit I am not), this wouldn't work. But at my current knowledge level it really, really does.

It's late and I have a headache but I hope this makes sense. This is a unique one for me.

item.title: SCP-5480: +1
item.content:encoded:
I can see some careless mistakes here or there, most obviously XXXXs all over the place. But honestly I think this was a funny article. It doesn't outlive its welcome, it doesn't do a lore dump. And ultimately this is well written, especially the dialogue upon which the entire article centers.

I hope this survives, I think its a welcome funny addition to the Sarkic lore (as a devotee to Sarkicism, I actually think a little bit of a lighter toned story is well overdue)… not to mention the idea of one of the object of a cult's worship not having the time or inclination to deal with the modern day cult is very appealing to me. Religion is mostly ridiculous, and holy stories are corrupted over time.

Not to mention the ending lines of this article are straight fire. I think its great, if could use a little cleaning up.

+1

item.title: SCP-5480:
item.content:encoded:
While I can see the merits of a funny article and or tale about klavigar saarn being fed up with modern sarkicism, this fails to make it work.

The article (minus interview) could be pretty much summed up as "this is the apartment of klavigar saarn from sarkicism. That one." In fact, you could probably replace the article entirely with those words and you wouldn't lose any narrative cohesiveness.

As for the interview, I don't really have much negative things to say about it. It's a bit odd that Saarn is talking like someone from the 21st century, but that's not really much of an issue. Unfortunately, I don't really have anything good to say either. Didn't really find it funny or otherwise appealing.

If the description portion of the article was better , maybe I could be convinced to novote this. But with the current state of it, it's a -1.

item.title: SCP-5031: There’s Some Fridge Horror Here
item.content:encoded:
Obviously I love the baby boy myself as well, but honestly what I love most about this is that there’s actually some rather troubling implications from this interaction.

The whole concept hinges on the idea that the first article written by the previous researcher was laughably inaccurate at describing the complexity of the creatures mentality and threat. It was because of this bad documentation that the thing was chucked into a box for ages and allowed to suffer for no reason. I would go so far as to say that the whole “attacks and consumes all creatures it encounters” is a straight up farce. It probably just hunted and killed things occasionally because despite not requiring sustenance it still seems to experience hunger and it just didn’t know any better than to attack humans. It had the mentality of a toddler after all. The whole first article is a very clever way at poking fun at the melodrama and boring simplicity of the generic murder monster trope on the site, but in universe the generic murder monster that must be kept in a box trope is presented here as a real problem within the foundation of researchers not taking the time to fully understand an anomaly beyond its base threats or to consider the well-being of said anomaly.

This begs the question: Just how many inaccurately recorded and unreasonably contained SCPS are there?? How many generic murder monsters on this site are actually products of a biased researcher making snap judgements about complex creatures? There could be any number of sentient beings harbored by the foundation that, with proper treatment, could also learn to become more than a monster in a cage. If an article as incredibly misleading as the one Huxtable contested could go uncontested for a whole decade, it makes you wonder if maybe there are a few other articles leaving out a few key details…

I overall like the concept because it executes it in a way that feels real. There are so many points where this could have gotten cringy cutesie or forced, but it very well balanced the idea of there being an alien and possibly dangerous monster who displays a capacity to learn and has an actual personality. It’s wholesome but not overly indulgent in that fact. So yeah, it makes me feel good reading it. I also just like the idea that this Huxtable guy is part of some kind of containment reform movement that’s gonna uncover a bunch of dumb things the foundation has done over the years. Judging from this article, they sorely need one.

Anyways, TLDR: Very clever way of turning the tropes we’re used to on its head. Could have been a bit more conflict but honestly I’m just glad this thing exists. +1

item.title: SCP-5900:
item.content:encoded: I feel like this hit in just the right place of "this author knows more than me on a subject, but they don't want me to feel stupid because of that." I think it works so well because the focus is really on that emotional state of "can't panic now, I've got too much to do," an experience I think most people have been through.
